title: 5 Tools for Fair Residency Call Schedules
description: Five tools for fair residency call schedules compared: Scheduling Wizard, Excel, QGenda, Amion and Lightning Bolt, by who does the counting.
content:
A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

Summary

  • Residency scheduling involves two distinct jobs: complex schedule creation and simple schedule viewing. Amion publishes the schedule and QGenda needs an operator at the program to build one; with either, someone on your side still owns the build and the fairness counts.
  • A Neurosurgery study found that a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70% and improved residents' perception of fairness from 43% to 95%.
  • With self-service software, configuration, fairness balancing and checking the ACGME rules sit with the chief resident; a managed service takes that work off the chief.
  • For programs looking to offload the administrative burden, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard builds schedules to your fairness rules and the ACGME requirements you tell us apply; whether they go into your existing platform, a live view we build, or both is entirely up to you.

Building a fair residency call schedule is one of the most thankless jobs in medicine. The process is a grueling manual exercise of counting shifts, juggling time-off requests, and wrestling with call pool gaps that often leaves residents feeling the schedule is unfair.

The first thing to sort out is whether you need help building the schedule or publishing it. Below are five options, compared on how each handles call fairness and the ACGME rules.

The 5 Tools for Residency Call Schedule Fairness

These tools range from fully managed services that take the chief resident's workload to self-service software that requires significant manual configuration.

1. Scheduling Wizard

  • Type: Managed Scheduling Service
  • Best For: Residency and fellowship programs that want to hand off the administrative burden of schedule creation and help institutional scheduling knowledge persist across annual chief rotations.

Scheduling Wizard is the one on this list that is a done-for-you managed service rather than software you operate yourself. The distinction is fundamental: there is nothing to log into; you send your rules. These include vacation requests, rotation rules, resident preferences, clinic dates, and coverage requirements. You then receive a complete schedule delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

  • Fairness: Scheduling Wizard is a team that builds physician schedules full time. Fairness isn't something you tune afterwards; it is one of the rules the schedule is built to. Our team handles Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules simultaneously, resolving cross-schedule dependencies that would take a human chief dozens of hours to untangle.
  • ACGME Compliance: The duty hour rules you tell us apply, subspecialty ones included, go into the schedule as it is built, not into a check afterwards. We build the rules in; the review at the end is a check, not a repair job.
  • Implementation Burden: Low. The chief resident's role shifts from schedule builder to schedule reviewer. There's no software to learn, no set of rules to configure, and no annual knowledge loss when the chief rotates out. The written rule set persists year over year.
  • Cost: Program-level pricing based on size and needs. Contact Scheduling Wizard for a quote.

Where the schedule lives is entirely up to you. Many programs upload our finished schedule into the platform they already use for daily viewing; others use the live view, or both.

What you get: the finished call schedule in the format your program asks for, Excel or Google Sheets, and a custom live view we build for you if you want one. Major redrafts are part of the engagement rather than an extra: when someone goes on leave, changes rotation or leaves mid-year, we rebuild around the gap. For the specifics, see our page on call schedule fairness. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel Spreadsheets

  • Type: Manual Tool
  • Best For: Programs that want full control and have a chief resident with the time to count and check everything by hand.

The spreadsheet is where many programs start, and where a lot of the scheduling stories on Reddit come from.

  • Fairness: Entirely manual. That means shift-counting, complex pivot table logic, and the constant anxiety that, as one resident puts it, “at any given point in the year it won’t be perfectly even.” Managing vacation-forced Q2 call stretches, golden weekend equity, and intern-versus-senior pool distributions by hand is exactly as painful as it sounds.
  • ACGME Compliance: None. The chief resident is solely responsible for manually tracking every duty hour rule, which is easy to get wrong under time pressure.
  • Implementation Burden: High. The chief resident is the scheduling system. It takes dozens of hours a year, and much of what the chief knew leaves with them at each transition.
  • Cost: Technically free, but expensive in resident time, morale cost, and compliance risk.

3. QGenda

  • Type: Self-Service Enterprise Software
  • Best For: Large health systems with dedicated administrative staff who can own the configuration.

QGenda is a well-known scheduling platform in academic medicine, feature-rich and integrated into many hospital workflows. It is a rules-based platform your team runs: you set up and maintain the rules, the platform helps produce and manage the schedule, and someone at the program reviews it.

  • Fairness: Depends on configuration. The platform can enforce the rules you set up and surface violations; how even your call ends up depends on how those rules are set and how much time goes into reviewing the result.
  • ACGME Compliance: User-managed. QGenda can be configured to flag potential ACGME duty hour violations, but building, maintaining, and verifying those rules is the program's responsibility. If your rules are misconfigured, violations slip through.
  • Implementation Burden: High. There is a lot to learn, which is hard to fit into a chief resident's one-year tenure. Significant upfront configuration and ongoing operational maintenance are required.
  • Cost: Contact the vendor for a quote.

4. Amion

  • Type: Publishing Platform with basic manual editing
  • Best For: Programs looking for a simple way to publish a schedule that has already been created through another process.

Amion comes up often in residency forums, and it is well liked for what it is: an easy way for residents to check their schedule, see who's on call, and manage swaps. The confusion arises when programs assume Amion also solves the schedule creation problem.

  • Fairness: Not its job. Amion publishes the schedule. Whatever fairness (or unfairness) exists in your call schedule is determined entirely by the manual process you used to build it beforehand, using a spreadsheet, institution-specific logic, or years of institutional tradition.
  • ACGME Compliance: None built in. Checking the schedule against the duty hour requirements happens wherever it is built, before it is published.
  • Implementation Burden: High for schedule creation, which happens outside the publishing step. Publishing the schedule is easy, but the dozens of hours of counting shifts, managing time-off requests, and fine-tuning call pool distributions still fall entirely on the chief. One forum contributor noted there are ways to export from Amion into a pivot table for more accurate shift counting, but the counting is still yours.
  • Cost: Contact the vendor for pricing.

5. Lightning Bolt (by PerfectServe)

  • Type: Self-Service Software with a Rules-Based Engine
  • Best For: Larger departments that want a more sophisticated self-service tool than Amion and are willing to invest in configuration to get schedule suggestions.

Lightning Bolt sits a step above purely manual tools by using a rules-based engine that can suggest assignments based on pre-configured rules. It's a meaningful step up from a blank spreadsheet for programs with someone to run it.

  • Fairness: The system can produce workable draft schedules based on your rules, and someone at the program reviews and adjusts the drafts before they go out.
  • ACGME Compliance: Semi-automated. Lightning Bolt can check against user-defined rules, but the final compliance verification is still the user's responsibility after reviewing the output.
  • Implementation Burden: Moderate to high. The chief resident must learn the platform, carefully define all rules and preferences, and invest ongoing time in managing schedule outputs. The operational burden doesn't disappear; it's just partially assisted.
  • Cost: Contact the vendor for pricing.

Building the Schedule vs Publishing It

There are two different jobs in residency scheduling, and conflating them leads to choosing the wrong tool entirely:

  1. Schedule Building. This is the hard task of building a fair, finished schedule from scratch, to the ACGME requirements that apply. This is where residency call schedule fairness is decided. It involves every rule, weighted distribution, duty hour limits and balance across every resident, rotation, and coverage requirement simultaneously.
  2. Publishing the Schedule. This is the day-to-day job of publishing a finished schedule so residents can see their assignments, check who's on call, and request swaps.

Amion is built for the second job. QGenda can help with the first, but someone at the program still runs it and owns the result. Either way, the first job stays with the program.

The first job is where fairness is decided. A study in Neurosurgery found that rebuilding the call schedule to written rules reduced call variation by 70% and improved residents' perception of schedule fairness from 43% to 95%.

Are You a Schedule Builder or a Schedule Reviewer?

Before choosing a tool, decide which job you are hiring it to do.

If you need help publishing a schedule, and you're comfortable building it yourself, Amion and QGenda are proven, widely-used solutions. They do that job well.

But if your goal is true residency call schedule fairness, counted rather than manually approximated, you need a tool built specifically for schedule building. Every self-service option on this list places the burden of fairness squarely on the person operating the software. The tool's sophistication only goes as far as your ability (and available time) to configure it.

A managed service moves the build off the program. Instead of spending weeks counting shifts, fine-tuning call pools, and manually verifying ACGME compliance, you spend a few hours reviewing a finished schedule that was built to be fair from the ground up. When the next chief steps in, the written rule set doesn't vanish with the outgoing one; it persists.

If your program is ready to hand off the scheduling burden, give your residents a schedule they can check for fairness, and get the ACGME rules built in without becoming a scheduling software expert, book a call and tell us how your call schedule works.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is Scheduling Wizard different from Amion?

Scheduling Wizard is a managed service that builds fair schedules to your rules for you, while Amion is a platform for publishing a schedule you have already built, and QGenda is software your team operates. Scheduling Wizard handles the hard job of schedule creation, delivering the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Whether you then upload it into your existing platform, use the live view, or both is entirely up to you.

How does Scheduling Wizard handle the ACGME rules?

Scheduling Wizard builds in the ACGME duty hour rules you tell us apply, and we check the finished schedule against them before it goes out. With self-service software your team configures the rules and reviews what the platform raises; we build the rules in first, so the review has far less to find.

Can you handle the specific ACGME rules for my subspecialty?

You tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and anything your specialty's Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you alongside your own rules before the first build. They go into the schedule while it is built rather than being flagged afterwards. We do not assume we know your requirements better than you do; we ask.

Do we have to stop using Amion to use Scheduling Wizard?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

What does "managed service" mean for the chief resident?

A managed service means the chief resident's role shifts from being a schedule builder to a schedule reviewer. Instead of spending dozens of hours learning software and manually building the schedule, you simply provide your program's inputs, like vacation requests, rotation rules and coverage needs, and we build the schedule and deliver the finished product to you, taking the administrative burden off you and helping scheduling knowledge persist year after year.
